title: Locality of Reference: Temporal and Spatial
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: Programs reuse what they have just used (temporal locality) and use things next to what they have just used (spatial locality). Cache exploits the first by keeping a line, and the second by fetching a whole block rather than a word.
remember: Temporal locality: an item accessed recently is likely to be accessed again soon - the same variable in a loop, the same instruction on the next iteration.
Spatial locality: an item near a recently accessed one is likely to be accessed soon - the next element of an array, the next instruction in sequence.
The unit of transfer is the block (line); the unit of addressing is the word or byte. That mismatch is deliberate: it is how spatial locality is bought.
Block size is the one knob that trades the two: a larger block exploits more spatial locality per miss but lowers the number of lines for a fixed cache size and raises the miss penalty.
A program with no locality - a random walk over a large array - defeats the cache; locality is a property of the program, not of the hardware.

example.prompt: A 16 KB direct-mapped cache has 32 B blocks. Loop 1 sums A[0..2047] of doubles in order; loop 2 sums the same array with a stride of 1024 elements. Which loop misses less?
example.work: 32 B holds 4 doubles, so loop 1 misses once per four elements: 2048/4 = 512 misses. Loop 2 steps 1024 doubles = 8192 B = 256 blocks apart, so each of its 2048 accesses touches a different block: 2048 misses.
example.answer: Loop 1: 512 misses against 2048 - the sequential loop buys spatial locality from the block, the strided loop buys nothing.

gateAngle: GATE tests locality through a miss count over a stated access sequence, not by asking for a definition. The pattern is always: work out which block each address belongs to, then count the first touch of each block.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: An 8 KB direct-mapped cache has 64 B blocks and a program reads every 4th byte of a 1 MB array once. How many misses?
variations.answer: A 64 B block covers 64 bytes, so every 16th read of the stride-4 walk falls in a new block: 262144 reads / 16 = 16384 blocks touched, and each misses once, so 16384 misses.
variations.why: It tests the distinction between the number of accesses and the number of distinct blocks, which is what spatial locality turns into a saving.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a larger block help instruction fetches more than data reads?
variations.answer: Instructions are fetched in sequence almost always, so the rest of the block is nearly certain to be used; data accesses jump, so the rest of a block may never be touched.
variations.why: It is the reason instruction and data caches are separate, and the reason early restart works best for instruction streams.

trap.what: Believing a bigger block always lowers the miss rate.
trap.why: Beyond a point the block becomes a large fraction of the cache, so the number of lines falls, competition for lines rises, and a line is evicted before its other words are used; the miss penalty also rises because more words must be transferred.
trap.counterexample: In a 1 KB cache, moving from 32 B to 512 B blocks leaves two lines; any two blocks that map to the same line now evict each other on every access.

check.question: A cache line holds 8 words and a program reads 8 consecutive words from the same line. How many misses does that cost, and how many would a 1-word line cost?
check.explanation: The first word misses and brings the whole line; the other seven hit. With a 1-word line every read is a separate miss - which is exactly the cost spatial locality removes.
